title: Basic system and network administration
content:
## Overview

FortiGate is a robust, multifunctional security device that can act in different modes or roles to address different network requirements. In today's complex environments, networks run vertically from the LAN to the internet, and horizontally from the physical network to the private virtual network and to the cloud. FortiGate can be deployed as a data-center firewall, as an ISFW to contain a network breach, and can also function as DNS and DHCP servers configured to provide web filter, antivirus, and IPS services.

![Basic system and network administration](diagram:0)

## Operating Modes

When you deploy FortiGate, you can choose between two operating modes:

- **NAT mode** (default): FortiGate routes packets based on layer 3, like a router. Each logical network interface has an IP address, and FortiGate determines the egress interface based on the destination IP address and entries in its routing tables.
- **Transparent mode**: FortiGate forwards packets at layer 2, like a switch. Its interfaces have no IP addresses, and FortiGate identifies the egress interface based on the destination MAC address. The device in transparent mode has an IP address used for management traffic.

NAT mode is the default operation mode. In each firewall policy, you can enable or disable UTM and NGFW modules.

## Initial Setup

To access the GUI on FortiGate or FortiWiFi, open a web browser and visit `https://192.168.1.99`. The default login information is public knowledge — never leave the default password blank.

All FortiGate models have a console port, or USB management port, or both. You can access the CLI using the CLI console widget on the GUI or from a terminal emulator such as PuTTY or Tera Term.

You can configure the **interface role** (WAN, LAN, Undefined). Settings that do not apply to the current role are hidden on the GUI, preventing accidental misconfiguration. For example, when the role is configured as WAN, there is no DHCP server and device detection configuration available. You can give interfaces **aliases** (for example, calling port3 `internal_network`) to make your list of policies easier to comprehend.

Interface IP addresses can be assigned:
- Manually (static)
- Automatically using DHCP
- Automatically using PPPoE (available on the CLI)

The built-in DHCP server supports advanced options including DNS servers, NTP configurations, DHCP relay to forward requests to an external server, and custom IP address assignment rules to map specific IP addresses to MAC addresses.

## Routing Configuration

Before integrating FortiGate into your network, you should configure a default gateway. You must configure a **static route** with destination `0.0.0.0/0` to forward traffic through the network interface connected to the internet. Without this, FortiGate will not be able to respond to packets outside the subnets directly attached to its own interfaces and may fail to connect to FortiGuard.

FortiGate hardware uses application-specific integrated circuits (ASIC) such as a content processor (CP) or network processor (NP) chip for cryptography and packet forwarding, delivering dramatically better performance compared to single-purpose devices.

> **Key terms:** RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is not a valid IP assignment method.

> **Key terms:** Setting the role to Undefined displays all options, including those normally hidden by other roles.
